Jeanie Buss Sues Siblings to Block Sale of LA Lakers Family Stake
Los Angeles Lakers governor Jeanie Buss has petitioned the Los Angeles Superior Court to block her five siblings from selling their remaining 17.8% stake in the franchise. The legal challenge aims to invalidate a recent vote by her siblings, arguing that any sale of the trust’s shares requires her consent.
The Legal Basis of the Buss Family Dispute
The conflict centers on the interpretation of the JAB Trust, the entity that holds the family’s ownership interest in the Los Angeles Lakers. According to a letter from attorney Adam Streisand, which was reviewed by CNBC, Jeanie Buss maintains that she is the controlling owner of the team, a status solidified by a 2017 court order. Streisand asserts that the co-trustees—Jeanie, Janie, and Joey Buss—are legally bound to vote the shares in a manner that ensures Jeanie maintains the minimum 15% ownership required to remain the team’s governor.
The siblings, however, have stated their intention to proceed with the sale. In a statement reported by ESPN and the BBC, Johnny, Jim, Janie, Joey, and Jesse Buss confirmed they remain united in their decision to sell the family’s remaining interest to an investment group led by former Disney CEO Bob Iger and financier Joshua Kushner. The potential buyers recently entered an agreement to purchase a majority stake from Mark Walter, who had acquired his interest from the Buss family last year.
Ownership Stakes and the $12.5 Billion Valuation
The financial stakes of this transaction are significant. The deal involving Mark Walter’s majority stake values the Los Angeles Lakers at approximately $12.5 billion, as reported by CNBC. The Buss family’s remaining 17.8% interest represents a substantial portion of the franchise’s equity. While the siblings argue that the sale is an appropriate exit strategy, Jeanie Buss contends that the move violates fiduciary duties and the established terms of the trust.
The disagreement places the future governance of the franchise in a state of uncertainty. For stakeholders and partners involved in high-stakes corporate disputes, the situation highlights the necessity of robust legal frameworks. When internal governance documents are challenged, parties often seek guidance from corporate litigation attorneys to interpret complex trust agreements and fiduciary obligations.
The Role of Fiduciary Duty in Sports Franchises
For those managing complex family assets or multi-generational business holdings, the current dispute underscores the importance of clear succession planning and defined decision-making protocols.
“The Los Angeles Lakers have never been just a basketball team. They have been one of the greatest privileges of our lives. Our focus has always been on what we believe is best for the Lakers, the fans who have supported this franchise for generations and the greater Los Angeles community,” the five siblings stated in their public response to the legal challenge.
Navigating Corporate Governance Challenges
As the legal proceedings in Los Angeles Superior Court move forward, the broader implications for the Lakers’ ownership structure remain unclear. The court must now determine if the 2017 order effectively grants Jeanie Buss veto power over the sale of the trust’s remaining interest. For organizations facing similar internal power struggles, securing expert counsel is the standard approach for mitigating risk.
Entities involved in high-value asset transfers or ownership disputes frequently rely on fiduciary advisory services to ensure compliance with court-mandated structures. Furthermore, as the court reviews the legality of the siblings’ vote, the necessity of maintaining transparent communication between shareholders becomes apparent. Organizations requiring assistance with complex documentation or regulatory filings often consult with corporate governance consultants to prevent similar deadlocks.
The court’s eventual ruling will not only decide the fate of the 17.8% stake but will also define the scope of control for the Lakers’ governor moving forward. Until a judicial resolution is reached, the potential sale remains stalled, leaving the future of the franchise’s ownership structure in the hands of the legal system.
